sentences.text: Judy loved tennis, but she was always nervous.
During big matches, her legs were shaking.
She often lost games because of her fear.
One day, Judy found a shop called Jingle Jump.
Mr. Jing, the owner, gave her a shimmering silver racket.
"This racket will guide you," he said.
The next day, Judy went to the court.
Suddenly, she heard a tiny whisper from the racket.
"Move right!
Hit now!" the whisper said clearly.
Judy followed the whisper.
She hit the ball perfectly.
She was surprised and very happy.
It was a winning shot.
With the silver racket, Judy won many matches.
She became well-known in her town.
However, she stopped practicing hard.
She only waited for the whispers.
Soon, Judy reached the championship finals.
Her opponent was Bella.
Bella was the best player and had very fast serves.
The whole stadium was filled with nervous excitement.
In the first set, Judy played well.
The silver racket told her what to do.
Judy felt like a star.
Bella was surprised by Judy's play.
During the second set, however, Judy tripped and fell.
The silver racket hit the ground.
It broke into two pieces.
Judy was shocked.
The magical whispers stopped.
Judy felt scared and alone.
"I can't win without the whispers," she thought.
She started to lose many points.
During the break, Judy sat on the bench.
She looked at her old, scratched racket in her bag.
It looked very dull and old.
She gripped the handle.
She saw the worn tape.
She remembered her long hours of practice.
Her hands were sore from working so hard.
Judy realized something important.
The whispers were not magic.
They were her own instincts.
She had learned them through many months of practice.
"The strength is inside me," Judy said.
She stood up and held her old racket tightly.
She did not need the silver racket anymore.
Judy returned to the court.
She played with her own rhythm.
She was not nervous anymore.
She moved fast and hit the ball with power.
The match was very close.
In the end, Bella won by a little.
Bella smiled and said, "That was a great game, Judy!"
Judy was happy.
She lost the trophy, but she found her confidence.
She knew she could play well with her own strength.

principles: Story Grammar structures what is assessed but is not treated as the sole model of reading comprehension.
Scores reflect evidence of Story Element and relationship understanding, not lexical or semantic similarity alone.
100/67/33/0 are operational reporting values; they are not empirically calibrated IRT ability estimates.
Overall feedback must be combined with the lowest skill profile and selected misconception.
